title: Verdant warmstart latency heuristics and microburst simulation (POC)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures the Verdant retail POC focused on warmstart/warm-cache heuristics for microburst workloads. Objective was to measure tail latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput under short spikes, and the cost impact of different warmup strategies on a realistic e-commerce traffic trace. The goal: find a small operational heuristic that reduces p99 tail during 1–5s microbursts with minimal steady-state cost.

Context and motivation:
- Customer (Verdant) uses chat-like product assistant with lots of short sessions and frequent cold intervals. Observed failures in production: p99 spikes during sudden promotional bursts (cart-checkout flow).
- Redwood features relevant to this POC: KV prefix cache, model quantization variants, routing fallback, and ability to send lightweight probe requests.
- Constraint: no persistent dedicated pool (they want low reserved capacity), so approach must work with hosted/dedicated hybrid routing and cost-sensitive heuristics.

Testbed and methodology:
- Models: open-llm-8B (fp16 baseline) and open-llm-8B-q4 (quantized) served as two compatible variants.
- Hardware: A100-40GB (baseline) and H100-80GB (experimental) instances via dedicated nodes.
- Serving runtime: Redwood v3.4.2 with KV cache enabled for first-token prefixes and continuous batching on.
- Synthetic trace: derived from Verdant production sample (anonymized) covering 48 hours; we synthesized 10,000 short sessions per hour with concentrated 30s promotional microbursts every 20 minutes. Also ran pure Poisson and diurnal traces for baseline.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 token latency, time-to-first-token (TTFT), throughput (tokens/s), CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, and estimated per-million-token cost (USD). Measurement periods: steady-state (outside bursts), burst window (0–60s), and recovery (60–300s).

Warmstart strategies evaluated:
1) Idle (no prewarm) — baseline behavior.
2) Periodic probe — small 16-token probe every 90s to keep minimal KV pages hot.
3) TTL-based keepalive — issue probe if last request > 120s.
4) Queue-drain prewarm — when average queue length > 5, send 32-token prewarm to a small pool; cancelable if actual user traffic arrives.
5) Hybrid: TTL + queue-drain + smart probed prefix selection (only top-10 prefixes by request frequency).

Key experimental findings (aggregated):
- Cold vs warm baseline: Cold requests (empty KV cache) increased p99 by ~3.8x compared to warm—average p99 cold token latency 1.1s on A100 vs warm 0.28s. TTFT was the largest contributor.
- Periodic probe (every 90s): Reduced p99 in bursts by ~22% vs Idle but increased steady-state cost by ~5%. KV hit rate improved from 62% to 78%.
- TTL-based keepalive (120s): Similar tail reduction (~20%) but fewer probes than periodic => cost +2.3% steady-state.
- Queue-drain prewarm: Most effective for short microbursts. When microburst starts (queue >5), a prewarm reduced p99 by up to 48% within the first 10s of the burst versus Idle. Cost impact was small when microbursts were infrequent because prewarm was conditional.
- Hybrid approach: Combined benefits — p99 reduction of ~45% during bursts while steady-state cost delta ~+3.1%. This produced the best overall cost/latency tradeoff.
- Quantized model behavior: The q4 variant had ~12–15% lower per-token latency when warmed, but cold-start p99 penalty was similar relative to its own warm baseline. Use-case: route bursty, latency-sensitive traffic to fp16 when p99 SLO is strict; otherwise q4 is better for cost.

Tail latency decomposition (qualitative):
- TTFT (kernel load, kv fetch): 55% of extra p99 during cold paths.
- Batch formation delay (waiting for tokens to batch): 20%. Continuous batching smoothing helped, but during microbursts very short sessions didn't accrue large batches.
- Model decode kernel time: 15% incremental.
- Queuing (backpressure) during severe spikes: 10% but dominated during sustained high load, not initial microburst.

Cost model and numbers (approx):
- Baseline Idle, mixed model, A100: $9.8 per 1M tokens.
- Hybrid warmstart + q4 routing: $8.1 per 1M tokens (due to quantization plus lower requeues), steady-state +3.1% overhead from probes.
- Queue-drain prewarm cost per incident: ~ $0.0035 for a single 32-token prewarm on A100. For 30 microbursts/day this is ~$0.11/day extra.

Operational recommendations (for Verdant POC):
1) Implement the Hybrid warmstart heuristic: TTL (120s) + conditional queue-drain prewarm + only probe top-10 prefixes. This balances p99 and cost.
2) Configure routing policy: during detection of promotional microburst (threshold: qlen > 5 and qps delta > 3x baseline), route a fraction (20%) of traffic to fp16 variant for lowest p99; default route stays q4. Use automatic fallback if fp16 capacity is saturated.
3) KV cache tuning: preserve first-16-token prefix pages for top-10 prefixes; increase KV cache TTL for those pages to 600s under heavy promotional schedules.
4) Metrics/alerts: create a p95/p99 regression alert on model route with 30m lookback and anomaly detection tied to burst windows. Instrument prewarm success rate and cancellation rate.
5) Runbook snippet for incidents: quick rollback to Idle probes -> scale-up dedicated nodes -> enable fp16 routing fallback.

Notes from the workshop session (10/15):
- Verdant ops expressed preference for minimal background probes due to compliance auditing; we agreed to keep probes observable and rate-limited per-region with audit logs.
- They asked for a simple UI toggle in Redwood Console for enabling/disabling prewarm heuristics per-route for quick experiments.
- Action item: engineering to expose KV-page top-k selection API (owner: Ravi Shah, JIRA-ENG-2142).

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Quantify impact on 95th percentile latency for sessions longer than 80 tokens (we focused on short sessions). Planned sweep next iteration. (Owner: Marina)
- Evaluate behavior when routing across heterogeneous hardware pools (A100 <-> H100) for warm cache affinity; current test slightly favors A100. (Owner: Noah)
- Verify audit compatibility for probe payloads with PII constraints — should use deterministic synthetic prompts. (Owner: Asha)

Immediate next steps (for the POC):
- Implement Hybrid heuristic in staging and run 7-day synthetic + production sampling test. (ETA: 2028-10-25)
- Add console control for per-route probe toggle and telemetry endpoint for prewarm events. (ETA: 2028-11-02)
- Deliver a short customer-facing write-up highlighting expected p99 reduction and steady-state cost delta. (ETA: 2028-11-05)

Appendix: quick command snippets
- Example probe payload (sanitized): {"input": "_probe_prefix_topK"} — use these tiny probes to warm KV pages without touching user PII.
- Suggested route config snippet: route{ name: "verdant-main", priority_policy: "latency-first", prewarm: {type: "hybrid", ttl_s: 120, queue_threshold: 5, top_k_prefixes: 10}}

Conclusions:
The Verdant POC shows that targeted warmstart heuristics (TTL + conditional prewarm + selective prefix probing) deliver meaningful p99 reductions for microburst workloads with low incremental cost. The hybrid approach is operationally practical for a hosted/dedicated hybrid deployment and aligns with Verdant’s desire for predictable tail latency during promotional events.

- 2028-10-18: consolidated results and runbook recommendations.
